newsitem.title: USA: Ross embarks Tuesday on new Mideast peace mission.
newsitem.headline: Ross embarks Tuesday on new Mideast peace mission.

text.p: U.S. Mideast envoy Dennis Ross planned to leave on Tuesday on a new mission to revive stalled Israeli-Palestinian peace negotiations, concerned about the climate between the two sides, a U.S. official said on Monday.
The atmosphere remains "sour," and the "psychological gaps may be more profound than the political" differences, an official familiar with Ross's thinking told Reuters.

John Dinger, a State Department spokesman, acknowledged that intensive efforts in recent weeks by President Bill Clinton, Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Ross and others to bring Israelis and Palestinians back into negotiations have so far failed.
"I cannot report any progress to you thus far," he told a news briefing.

Dinger said Ross would depart for the Middle East on Tuesday. He gave no details but other officials said Ross planned to meet on arrival first with the Israelis and then with Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat.
Dinger said Ross had a pattern of being flexible in his schedule but a senior official said privately that Ross expected to be back in Washington within a week.
Ross "is continuing the process that's been going on for perhaps about the last month, trying in particular to see what the parties are willing to do to get the process going," Dinger said.

Ross continues to act mainly as a mediator whose "prime function is always to get the parties to find room for agreement (but) that does not mean that he doesn't also have some ideas that he takes with him ... But yes, he does carry ideaS with him certainly," Dinger said without elaborating.

Dinger refused comment on a Egyptian newspaper report that Ross would carry a new demand that Israel cease all settlement activity in East Jerusalem, which has angered Palestinians and eroded their confidence in Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's commitment to their peace agreement.
But Dinger repeated the U.S. view that settlement activity was "unhelpful" to the peace process.
The peace process hit a crisis in March after Netanyahu gave bulldozers the green light to break ground for a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on land claimed by Israel and the Palestinians.

U.S. officials said there were no plans for Ross to try to revive peace negotiations between Israel and Syria, which are also stalled. Ross is known to believe that there must be progress on the Israeli-Palestinian track before talks between Jerusalem and Damascus can resume.

In a related matter, Dinger said the United States remained "very concerned" about the Israeli practice of stripping East Jerusalem Arabs of their legal papers but so far has not been able to persuade Israel to halt the practice, particularly as it relates to Palestinians who hold American passports.
"We have been particularly concerned about that issue and to the degree that it relates to Palestinian Americans, who have been affected by those policies," Dinger said.
He said the United States had "repeatedly raised the issue with the Israeli government, including at the highest levels."
Dinger cited "reports" that Israel would alter the practice but said the issue of Palestinians with American passports, in any event, had not yet been resolved.
"It is an issue that must be addressed," he said.
Critics say Israel's confiscation of identity cards is aimed at forcing Palestinian departures from East Jerusalem.
